thread.title: Ams AG Is Biggest Winner in Apple’s 3-D Sensing, Says Bernstein

author: Tiernan Ray
title: Ams AG Is Biggest Winner in Apple’s 3-D Sensing, Says Bernstein
text:
By Tiernan Ray Updated April 10, 2018 2:14 p.m. ET The big winner from Apple ’s ( AAPL ) increased use of “ 3-D sensing ” in the iPhone is not Lumentum ( LITE ) and those other laser companies you’ve heard about, writes David Dai of Bernstein today.
It’s the Austrian manufacturer Ams AG ( AMS ), whose shares he starts today with an Outperform rating,
3-D sensing, part of augmented reality , makes possible things such as the " Face ID ” function that recognizes your face on the iPhone X.
Ams is already a “key supplier” to Apple, writes Dai. The company makes something called an “ optical path ” for the iPhone X.
The optical path sits in front of the lasers that are provided by Lumentum or possibly a company such as F inisar ( FNSR ). It helps guide the beams of the lasers in the iPhone X’s front-facing “True Depth” camera that produces Face ID:
In the iPhone front 3D sensor, ams supplies an optical path that is the crucial component of iPhone dot projector (Exhibit 8). The purpose of the optical path, which sits on top of the VCSEL laser source, is to project 30,000-dot light patterns which enables 3D sensing. The optical path is a highly-integrated, high-precision optical component that integrates wafer level optics (WLO) lens, glass mirrors, and an active diffractive optical element (DOE). This requires expertise in optical lens design and manufacturing and miniaturized optics packaging. So far ams is the only company that can supply this component, and we believe it will remain the sole supplier at least in the next two years. In fact, we believe the front 3D sensor supply chain to be largely stable.
See the illustration at the bottom of this post for further on that.
Ams, notes Dai, is the sole provider of that part, which costs Apple $4, and he thinks prices are going to go higher this year because the part has to be refined: "There is room for further growth because the current iPhone 3D sensor is far from being perfect. There are many reports on iPhone X face recognition can't tell twins or even mother and child apart."
Dai, like others, expects 3D sensing to spread to the front of all of Apple’s iPhone models , which will cause the revenue from that part to surge for Ams: "This year, assuming all new iPhones will have front-facing 3D sensors, the revenue will roughly triple, and contribute 40% of Ams' revenues by 2018."
But Dai sees an even more powerful future for the company: as 3D sensing is built into the back of the iPhone , and phones from other vendors, those phones need a more powerful VCSEL laser than those provided by Finisar or Lumentum or the other big vendor, II-VI ( IIVI ).
He thinks Ams will scoop up that business because it has the superior technology thanks to the its acquisition last summer of Princeton Optronics .
His assumption they’ll get the rear-laser business is controversial, he acknowledges:
We believe that ams will supply (and most likely sole-supply) the VCSEL5 laser source for the new iPhone rear 3D sensor in 2H19 (Exhibit 11 and Exhibit 12). We understand that this is a bold assertion, but there is evidence that ams, as well as AAC, Largan, Sony, are all suggesting rear 3D sensor in 2H19 for a large OEM, which we believe is Apple. For ams, it is building a factory in Singapore which will mass produce VCSEL in mid 2019, so the timing matches the 2H19 iPhone production well. This can't be just coincidental. We currently expect 1/3 of the new iPhones in 2019 will have rear 3D sensors, which is similar to 2017, when 1/3 of the new iPhones had front 3D sensors (iPhone X).
This means an additional $4 to $5 for every iPhone with the rear-side capability, starting in 2019, writes Dai:
For the VCSEL ams will supply to iPhone rear 3D sensor, we model the ASP to be $4.50, given that the current iPhone front 3D VCSEL already costs US$4-4.5. This is a conservative assumption, because the VCSEL in the rear 3D sensor should be multiple times more powerful than that of front 3D sensor in order to reach further distances. The higher power would translate into larger die size and hence higher price. There are a few factors that would enable some cost savings from ams' VCSEL solution: First, the superior technology of ams (Princeton Optronics) enables much tighter pitch (10 micron vs typical 40 micron of competitors), which means smaller VCSEL die with the same number of VCSELs. Secondly, the current front 3D sensor VCSEL features a pseudo-random array to form a pattern, so the VCSELs are not as tightly arranged as they could be. In the rear 3D sensor, the VCSEL array does not need to form a pattern, and hence can be arranged more tightly. These factors contribute to cost savings. With these savings, we still think the US$4.5 ASP is very conservative.
Dai assigns a price target of 180 Swiss Franks to the shares, which are traded on the Swiss stock exchange.
Shares of Ams are up 3.94 Swiss francs today, or 4%, at Fr. 103.00.
